finding.claim: Missing authorization on DELETE /files/<fid>: require_allowed is an alias for is_allowed, which only returns a boolean. The result is discarded, so any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated or unprivileged HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with a known file id.

trace.note: from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed; this is the boolean predicate, not ensure_allowed
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') is called and its return value is ignored, so no abort(403) happens
is_allowed returns True or False and never aborts

finding.guards_checked: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8) would abort(403), but it is not used on this route. The before_request hook does no authentication check. No other decorator or middleware is present.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: is_allowed (acl.py:4) returns a bool only; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8) aborts but is not used on the delete route; before_request (views.py:11) only reads a header and does no check
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean is_allowed as require_allowed, views.py:18 discards its result, and views.py:19 runs `del STORE[fid]` unconditionally for any client, authenticated or not, who knows a file id (acl.py:4 never aborts).

finding.claim: Authentication is a client-supplied header taken as the user identity. The header X-Session-User-Verified is read directly with no session or signature validation, so any client can impersonate any user, including on the rename route that is otherwise ACL-protected.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') on rename, and the user identity check in general

trace.note: g.user is set from the raw request header
g.user is used as the ACL principal in ensure_allowed
grants are looked up by the user string, so a spoofed owner name gets the owner's grants

finding.guards_checked: No verification of the header, no session, and no signing. The name suggests a trusted upstream proxy sets it, but nothing in the code strips or validates it. If a trusted gateway overwrites the header, this is mitigated. That is not visible in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo. The only check is ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), which aborts 403 correctly, but it takes the spoofed g.user as the principal. No header stripping, session or signature check exists. A trusted upstream gateway that overwrites the header would mitigate this, but that is outside the repo.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the X-Session-User-Verified request header, views.py:26 passes it to ensure_allowed, and acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, so any anonymous client who sends the owner's name gets the owner's write grant. The only mitigation would be an external proxy that overwrites the header, which this code does not show.
